questions.question: A peripheral blood smear was made when a CBC was ordered on a 66-year-old female scheduled to undergo a hernia repair. Many small, mature lymphocytes were seen. Her Hgb was 12.8, Hct 36.9, MCV 88, platelet count 179,000, and WBC count 30,500. The best diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: An isolated, significantly elevated white blood cell count comprised overwhelmingly of small, morphologically mature-appearing (though functionally incompetent) lymphocytes in an asymptomatic elder...

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Septic shock:
options: Presence of foreign body in the blood
Characterized by peripheral pulling of blood
questions.explanation: الصدمة الإنتانية (Septic shock) تحدث نتيجة تجرثم الدم (Septicemia) وإفراز البكتيريا لسمومها الداخلية (Endotoxins)، مما يؤدي إلى توسع وعائي جهازي وهبوط حاد في ضغط الدم.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Atherosclerosis:
options: Thickening of media that lead to narrowing of vessel lumen
questions.explanation: التصلب العصيدي (Atherosclerosis) يتميز بتكوين لويحات عصيدية (Atheromas) في الطبقة الداخلية (Intima) للشرايين، مما يؤدي إلى تضيق التجويف وإضعاف الجدار. السمك يحدث في البطانة وليس الطبقة الوسطى.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Edema means:
options: Normal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces
Abnormal accumulation of excess fluid in the intracellular spaces
Abnormal accumulation of the fluid in the visceral cavities
Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces and visceral cavities
questions.explanation: الوذمة (Edema) تُعرّف بأنها التراكم غير الطبيعي للسوائل في الأنسجة الخلالية (Interstitial spaces)، وعندما تتجمع في التجاويف الجسمية تُسمى انصباباً (Effusion).

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Congestion means:
options: Increased the volume of blood in the particular tissue
Increased the volume of deoxygenated blood due to impaired venous outflow
Passive process of collection of blood in aortic aneurysm
Decrease in blood volume in a tissue
questions.explanation: الاحتقان (Congestion) هو عملية سلبية تنتج عن ضعف تصريف الدم الوريدي (Impaired venous outflow)، مما يؤدي إلى تراكم الدم غير المؤكسج في الأنسجة.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis:
options: Developed in the deep pelvic vein or leg veins
questions.explanation: الخثار الوريدي العميق (DVT) يحدث غالباً في الأوردة العميقة للساقين أو الحوض، ويعتبر المصدر الرئيسي والأكثر خطورة للصمات الرئوية (Pulmonary embolism).

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: What type of embolism passes through a small opening between left and right sides of the heart:
questions.explanation: الصمة التناقضية (Paradoxical embolism) تحدث عندما تنتقل الصمة من الجانب الأيمن للقلب إلى الجانب الأيسر (أو العكس) عبر عيب خلقي في الحاجز القلبي، لتصل إلى الدورة الشريانية الجهازية.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Most common causes of acute ischemia:
questions.explanation: الانسداد الشرياني المفاجئ الذي يؤدي إلى نقص التروية الحاد (Acute ischemia) ينتج في الغالب عن تكون جلطة موضعية (Thrombosis) أو انتقال صمة (Embolism) تسد الوعاء الدموي.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Vascular hyperemia:
options: Active process due to arteriolar dilation
Passive process due to venous obstruction
questions.explanation: فرط الدم (Hyperemia) هو عملية نشطة (Active process) تحدث بسبب توسع الشرايين لزيادة تدفق الدم المؤكسج، كما يلاحظ في الالتهابات أو أثناء ممارسة الرياضة.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Which of the following cause splenic congestion:
questions.explanation: احتقان الطحال ينتج غالباً عن ارتفاع ضغط الدم البابي (Portal hypertension)، والذي يعيق التصريف الوريدي من الطحال ويؤدي إلى تضخمه واحتقانه بالدم.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Gandy-Gamma nodules present in which of the following:
questions.explanation: عقد غاندي غامنا (Gandy-Gamna nodules) هي بؤر صغيرة من التليف وترسب الهيموسيديرين والكالسيوم، وتُعد علامة مميزة للاحتقان المزمن في الطحال (Chronic congestive splenomegaly).

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: All are seen in chronic lung venous congestion except:
questions.explanation: الاحتقان الوريدي المزمن للرئة يتميز بوجود وذمة، نزيف مجهري، وبلاعم محملة بالهيموسيديرين (خلايا فشل القلب). التغير الدهني (Steatosis) يحدث أساساً في الكبد كاستجابة لنقص الأكسجة أو السموم.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Occlusion of left middle cerebral artery by septic embolism cause:
questions.explanation: احتشاء الدماغ الناتج عن انسداد الشرايين (مثل الشريان الدماغي الأوسط) يؤدي بشكل فريد إلى نخر تمييعي (Liquefactive necrosis) بدلاً من النخر المتخثر الذي يحدث في باقي الأعضاء الصلبة.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Fat embolism:
questions.explanation: الصمة الدهنية (Fat embolism) ترتبط بشكل وثيق بكسور العظام الطويلة (مثل عظم الفخذ) أو الرضوض الشديدة للأنسجة الرخوة، حيث تتسرب قطرات الدهون من النخاع إلى مجرى الدم.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Blood accumulation in body cavity:
questions.explanation: تراكم الدم داخل تجاويف الجسم يسمى بناءً على موقعه، مثل تدمي التامور (Hemopericardium) في تجويف القلب، أو تدمي الصدر (Hemothorax) في التجويف الجنبي.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: The characteristic feature of pathogenesis of thrombosis is:
options: Adhesion of platelets on the subendothelial collagen
questions.explanation: إصابة البطانة الدموية (Endothelial injury) هي العامل الأهم في تكون الجلطات، حيث تؤدي إلى كشف الكولاجين تحت البطاني، مما يحفز التصاق وتنشيط الصفائح الدموية لبدء عملية التخثر.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: The difference between hyperemia and congestion:
options: Hyperemia occurs due to arterial dilation, congestion occurs due to venous obstruction
Hyperemia causes coldness, congestion causes warmth
Hyperemia is always pathological, congestion is always physiological
questions.explanation: فرط الدم (Hyperemia) هو عملية نشطة ناتجة عن توسع الشرايين (Arteriolar dilation)، بينما الاحتقان (Congestion) هو عملية سلبية تنتج عن إعاقة التدفق الوريدي (Venous obstruction).

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Origin of pulmonary emboli:
options: Thrombus of deep veins of the leg
questions.explanation: الغالبية العظمى من الصمات الرئوية (Pulmonary emboli) تنشأ من انفصال جلطات متكونة في الأوردة العميقة للساقين أو الحوض (DVT) وانتقالها عبر الجانب الأيمن للقلب إلى الرئتين.

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: Types of embolism involves a detached solid, liquid, gaseous mass carried by the bloodstream to distant site:
questions.explanation: الصمة (Embolus) يمكن أن تكون بأشكال فيزيائية متعددة: صلبة (مثل الجلطات المنفصلة Thromboembolism)، سائلة (مثل الصمة السلوية Amniotic fluid)، أو غازية (مثل صمة الهواء Air embolism).

questions.topic: أسئلة طبية حول الأوعية الدموية والتخثر
questions.question: What is the mechanism of thrombosis that leads to partly restoration of blood flow:
questions.explanation: إعادة الاستقناء أو الفتح (Recanalization) هي عملية ضمن مآلات الجلطة المزمنة، حيث تتكون قنوات وعائية جديدة داخل الجلطة المنظمة مما يسمح باستعادة جزئية لتدفق الدم عبر الوعاء المسدود.

questions.question: Most common cause lead to death in men:
questions.explanation: يُعتبر سرطان الرئة (Lung cancer) السبب الأول والوحيد الأكثر شيوعاً للوفيات المرتبطة بالسرطان لدى الرجال على مستوى العالم، ويُعزى ذلك أساساً إلى التدخين.

questions.question: Regarding anaplastic cells all true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: تتميز الخلايا الكشمية (Anaplastic cells) بأنويتها الكبيرة مفرطة الانصباغ وتعدد أشكالها (Pleomorphism)، ولا يقتصر شكلها على كونها "طويلة" بل تتخذ أشكالاً متغيرة وشاذة.

questions.question: Which virus causes nasopharyngeal cancer?
questions.explanation: فيروس إبشتاين بار (EBV) هو فيروس مسرطن بيولوجي يرتبط بقوة بتطور سرطان البلعوم الأنفي (Nasopharyngeal carcinoma) ولمفوما بيركيت.

questions.question: All are Childhood cancers except:
questions.explanation: في حين أن الساركوما العضلية المخططة، والساركوما العظمية، والأرومة الشبكية هي سرطانات تظهر عادة في الطفولة، فإن الأورام السرطاوية (Carcinoid tumors) هي أورام عصبية صماوية تظهر عادة عند البالغين.

questions.question: Rodent ulcer is caused by:
questions.explanation: سرطان الخلايا القاعدية (BCC) في الجلد يميل إلى الغزو الموضعي البطيء وتكوين قرحة خشنة ذات حواف مرتفعة، تُعرف سريرياً بالقرحة القارضة (Rodent ulcer).

questions.question: Azo dye lead to:
questions.explanation: الأصباغ الآزوية (Azo dyes) والأمينات العطرية هي مواد كيميائية مسرطنة تُطرح وتتركز في البول، مما يؤدي إلى تطور سرطان المثانة البولية.

questions.question: Normal cell with wrong located position:
questions.explanation: الورم المُنتبذ (Choristoma) هو شذوذ خلقي يتكون من أنسجة طبيعية وناضجة تماماً ولكنها تتواجد في موقع غير طبيعي (Ectopic)، مثل وجود نسيج بنكرياسي في المعدة.

questions.question: One of the following is a mixed tumor:
questions.explanation: الورم المسخي (Teratoma) هو ورم يتكون من أنواع متعددة من الأنسجة مشتقة من طبقات جرثومية مختلفة، مما يجعله مثالاً بارزاً على الأورام المختلطة.

questions.question: All of the following are inherited autosomal dominant tumors except:
questions.explanation: جفاف الجلد المصطبغ (Xeroderma pigmentosum) هو مرض وراثي جسدي متنحي (Autosomal recessive) ناتج عن خلل في جينات إصلاح الحمض النووي، على عكس الأورام الأخرى السائدة.

questions.question: The main diagnostic feature difference between benign and malignant:
questions.explanation: في حين أن النمو الغازي قوي في الإشارة إلى الخباثة، فإن القدرة على إحداث النقائل البعيدة (Metastasis) هي السمة القاطعة والأكثر دقة التي تثبت أن الورم خبيث، حيث أن الأورام الحميدة لا تنتشر أبداً.

questions.question: Grading of neoplasia is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: تحديد درجة الورم (Tumor grading) يتم حصراً عبر الفحص المجهري (Microscopic picture) لتقييم درجة التمايز، ومستوى الكشم الخلوي، والنشاط الانقسامي للخلايا.

questions.question: Perineural invasion occurs with:
questions.explanation: الغزو الموضعي للأعصاب (Perineural invasion) هو نمط غزو مجهري شائع ومميز للسرطانات الظهارية الخبيثة (Carcinomas)، مثل سرطان البروستاتا والبنكرياس.

questions.question: Tumors that commonly spread with lymph node:
questions.explanation: السرطانات الظهارية (Carcinomas) مثل سرطان الخلايا الحرشوفية تنتشر في مراحلها الأولى بشكل أساسي عبر الأوعية اللمفاوية إلى العقد اللمفاوية المجاورة.

questions.question: Malignant tumors are:
questions.explanation: تتميز الأورام الخبيثة بدرجات متفاوتة من فقدان التمايز (Anaplasia)، حيث يمكن أن تتراوح من جيدة التمايز، إلى ضعيفة التمايز، أو غير متمايزة تماماً (Undifferentiated/Anaplastic).

questions.question: The most important feature of malignant tumor is:
questions.explanation: تعتبر النقائل البعيدة (Metastasis) العلامة الوحيدة التي تميز الورم الخبيث بشكل مطلق عن الورم الحميد، حيث لا تنتشر الأورام الحميدة إلى أعضاء بعيدة أبداً.

questions.question: pTis N0 Mx means:
options: Regional lymph nodes are not examined
Carcinoma in situ, no lymph node involvement, metastasis cannot be assessed
questions.explanation: في نظام تحديد مراحل الورم (TNM)، يرمز pTis إلى سرطان موضعي غير غازي (Carcinoma in situ)، ويرمز N0 إلى عدم وجود انتشار في العقد اللمفاوية، بينما يرمز Mx إلى أن وجود النقائل البعيدة لا يمكن تقييمه.

questions.question: A Polyp is:
questions.explanation: السليلة (Polyp) هو مصطلح شكلي يصف نمواً بارزاً (Exophytic) أو نتوءاً يشبه الإصبع يبرز من سطح الغشاء المخاطي نحو التجويف، ويمكن أن يكون حميداً أو خبيثاً.

questions.question: In viral carcinogenesis one of the following is correct:
options: The host immunity can be decreased
Epstein-Barr virus causes ano-genital carcinoma and lymphoma
Carcinogenic virus genome is always incorporated in the host genome
Only DNA viruses can cause cancers
questions.explanation: نقص المناعة يقلل من المراقبة المناعية (Immune surveillance) التي تدمر الخلايا المصابة أو غير الطبيعية، مما يزيد بشكل كبير من خطر تكون الأورام بواسطة الفيروسات المسرطنة.

questions.question: The most important sign of malignancy is:
questions.explanation: بينما تعتبر علامات الكشم (Anaplasia) مثل تعدد الأشكال مهمة، فإن الغزو الموضعي للأنسجة (Invasiveness) والقدرة على إحداث النقائل هما السمتان الأهم والأكثر حسماً للتمييز بين الورم الخبيث والحميد.

questions.question: Which of the following acts as a dominant gene in cancer development?
questions.explanation: الجينات الورمية الأولية (Proto-oncogenes) تتطلب طفرة في أليل واحد فقط (Dominant) لتصبح جينات ورمية نشطة (Oncogenes) تعزز التكاثر الخلوي غير المنضبط.

questions.question: Which of the following requires mutation of both alleles (recessive) to promote cancer?
questions.explanation: الجينات الكابتة للورم (Tumor suppressor genes) مثل Rb و p53، تتطلب تثبيط أو طفرة في كلا الأليلين (فقدان الوظيفة) لكي تفقد قدرتها على منع تكاثر الخلايا.

questions.question: Which of the following genes normally stimulate cellular proliferation?
questions.explanation: الجينات الورمية الأولية (التي تتحول إلى Oncogenes) هي في الأصل جينات تنظيمية طبيعية تعزز وتحفز نمو الخلايا وتمايزها بشكل طبيعي.

questions.question: Which of the following genes normally inhibit cellular proliferation?
questions.explanation: الجينات الكابتة للورم (Tumor suppressor genes) تعمل كمكابح طبيعية تمنع نمو الخلايا غير المنضبط وتوقف تقدم دورة الخلية عند وجود خلل.

questions.question: P53 is classified as:
questions.explanation: يُعد جين p53 الجين الكابت للورم (Tumor suppressor gene) الأهم والأكثر عرضة للطفرات في السرطانات البشرية، ويُلقب بـ "حارس الجينوم" لقدرته على إيقاف دورة الخلية لإصلاح الـ DNA.

questions.question: Genes that normal cellular genes which repair damaged DNA are called:
questions.explanation: جينات إصلاح الحمض النووي (DNA repair genes) هي فئة رابعة منفصلة من الجينات التنظيمية، وتؤدي طفراتها إلى عدم استقرار الجينوم وتراكم الطفرات.

questions.question: Genes that regulate programmed cell death are called:
questions.explanation: جينات الموت الخلوي المبرمج (Apoptosis genes) مثل BCL-2 و BAX مسؤولة عن تنظيم عملية التخلص من الخلايا التالفة التي لا يمكن إصلاحها.

questions.question: Mutation in which of the following genes can lead to cancer?
questions.explanation: تطور السرطان هو عملية متعددة الخطوات تتطلب تراكماً لطفرات جينية في كل من الجينات المحفزة للنمو (Oncogenes) والجينات الكابتة للورم (Suppressor genes).

questions.question: The following pediatric malignancies are common at age of four years except:
questions.explanation: أورام الأرومة العصبية (Neuroblastoma)، والأرومة الشبكية (Retinoblastoma)، وابيضاض الدم الليمفاوي الحاد (ALL) هي سرطانات طفولة كلاسيكية، بينما يظهر سرطان الغدد الليمفاوية لهودجكين عادة في البالغين ا...

questions.question: Neoplasm is:
options: Normal proliferation of the epithelial cell
Collection of abnormal fluid in intercellular spaces
Autonomous, uncontrolled proliferation of the cells
questions.explanation: التنشؤ (Neoplasia) يُعرّف مرضياً بأنه نمو جديد وتكوين كتلة غير طبيعية نتيجة تكاثر خلوي مستقل (Autonomous) وغير منضبط بسبب طفرات جينية دائمة.

questions.question: A mass arising from breast and fixed to the chest wall, with swelling of the axilla in the same side. Which of the following masses indicate the proper diagnosis:
questions.explanation: التثبيت بجدار الصدر يمثل غزواً موضعياً عميقاً، وتورم الإبط يمثل انتشاراً لمفاوياً؛ وهما علامتان كلاسيكيتان لسرطان الثدي الغازي، وهو سرطان غدي (Adenocarcinoma).

questions.question: The following are benign neoplasms except:
questions.explanation: الورم المنوي (Seminoma) هو سرطان خبيث ينشأ من الخلايا الجرثومية في الخصية، وهو استثناء كلاسيكي لقاعدة تسمية الأورام، حيث ينتهي باللاحقة (oma-) رغم خباثته.

questions.question: A palpable nodule in the dome of the uterus of six year duration and silent features. The nodule most likely represents:
questions.explanation: المدة الطويلة (ست سنوات) وغياب الأعراض يشيران بوضوح إلى ورم حميد وبطيء النمو؛ وفي الرحم، يكون الورم العضلي الأملس الحميد (Leiomyoma) هو الأكثر شيوعاً.

questions.question: Which of the following tumors composed of more than one type of parenchymal cells?
questions.explanation: الأورام المسخية (Teratomas / Teratocarcinomas) هي أورام خاصة تتكون من أنواع متعددة من الخلايا والأنسجة الناضجة أو غير الناضجة المشتقة من أكثر من طبقة جرثومية واحدة.

questions.question: The following are regulatory genes for neoplasms except:
options: Gene that regulate amino acid arrangement in complement system
questions.explanation: الجينات التنظيمية الأربعة المرتبطة بتطور السرطان هي: الجينات الورمية، الجينات الكابتة للورم، جينات الاستماتة، وجينات إصلاح الـ DNA. جينات النظام المتمم لا تلعب دوراً مباشراً في التنشؤ.

questions.question: Malignant cell characterized microscopically by the following except:
questions.explanation: الخلايا الخبيثة تظهر كشماً (Anaplasia) يتميز بزيادة نسبة النواة إلى السيتوبلازم (N:C ratio) لتصبح قريبة من 1:1، بدلاً من النسبة الطبيعية المنخفضة 1:6.

questions.question: Synthetic pyramid and purine are for:
questions.explanation: نظائر البيورين والبيريميدين الاصطناعية هي مضادات استقلاب (Antimetabolites) تستخدم كأدوية علاج كيميائي (Chemotherapy) لمنع تخليق الـ DNA في الخلايا السرطانية سريعة الانقسام.

questions.question: The most common cancer in elderly:

A microcytic anemia from total body iron depletion
A mild to moderate normocytic or microcytic anemia in chronic systemic disease, with abundant...
A hemolytic anemia with raised reticulocytes
questions.explanation: Iron is present but cannot be used.

questions.question: Hepcidin causes functional iron deficiency by degrading which structure?
options: Ferroportin, the iron export channel on enterocytes and macrophages
questions.explanation: It blocks iron export from gut cells and macrophages.

questions.question: What MCV and smear pattern is typical of anemia of chronic disease?
questions.explanation: The blockade usually causes a mild anemia before severe microcytosis.

questions.question: In a patient with anemia of chronic disease, what usually dominates the clinical picture?
options: The underlying inflammatory, infectious or malignant disease
questions.explanation: The anemia itself is usually mild.

questions.question: A 4-year-old child presents with fatigue, fever, bone pain and easy bruising. The peripheral smear shows >20% blasts with scanty cytoplasm and inconspicuous nucleoli; MPO is negative and TdT is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MPO negative excludes myeloid origin, and TdT marks immature lymphoid cells.

questions.question: A 16-year-old male presents with an anterior mediastinal mass and lymphoblasts in the marrow. Which genetic abnormality is most characteristic of this leukemia?
questions.explanation: Think of the T-cell variant of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

questions.question: A bone marrow smear shows myeloblasts with prominent nucleoli and needle-like azurophilic granules. Cytochemistry is MPO positive and Sudan Black B positive; flow cytometry shows CD13, CD33 and CD117. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Auer rods are never seen in ALL.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with mucosal bleeding and a prolonged PT/aPTT. The marrow shows blasts with Auer rods and t(15;17). What is the mechanism of her life-threatening coagulopathy?
options: Hypogammaglobulinemia causing consumption of clotting factors
Release of primary granules from abnormal promyelocytes triggering DIC
questions.explanation: The granules of the malignant promyelocytes are the trigger.

questions.question: In acute promyelocytic leukemia, the PML-RARA fusion gene blocks myeloid maturation at which stage?
questions.explanation: The subtype's name tells you the stage.

questions.question: According to WHO 2022, which scenario is sufficient to diagnose AML even if the blast count is below 20%?
options: 12% blasts that are MPO positive without any genetic abnormality
questions.explanation: t(15;17), t(8;21) and inv(16) are examples of defining genetic abnormalities.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the WHO 2022 definition of AML with myelodysplasia-related changes?
options: It requires defining cytogenetic abnormalities or specific defining mutations; morphology alone...
It is diagnosed by morphologic dysplasia alone
It replaces the category of AML defined by differentiation
It requires a preceding diagnosis of CML
questions.explanation: The definition moved from morphology toward genetics.

questions.question: Which cytochemical profile is expected in acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
options: TdT negative, MPO positive, PAS negative
TdT positive, MPO negative, PAS positive
TdT positive, MPO positive, Sudan Black B positive
TdT negative, MPO negative, PAS negative
questions.explanation: One of these enzymes helps exclude myeloid lineage.

questions.question: Flow cytometry of a lymphoblast population shows CD2, CD3, CD5 and CD7 positivity along with TdT. Which leukemia is this?
questions.explanation: CD10, CD19 and CD20 would point to the other lineage.

questions.question: Which sites are frequently involved by extramedullary spread in ALL?
questions.explanation: Think of the sites that need prophylactic attention in ALL.

questions.question: A patient with AML of monocytic differentiation presents with gum swelling and violaceous skin nodules. These findings represent which pair?
options: Auer rods and anterior mediastinal mass
questions.explanation: Both are tissue infiltrations seen in monocytic subtypes.

questions.question: Which inherited condition shows a strong association with ALL, particularly in children older than 5 years?
questions.explanation: A trisomy syndrome carries a markedly raised leukemia risk.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man has an incidental WBC of 150,000/µL with a full spectrum of granulocyte maturation, absolute basophilia and massive splenomegaly. Which pair of findings is expected?
options: High LAP score and t(9;22) / BCR-ABL1
Low LAP score and CD5+/CD23+ lymphocytes
Low LAP score and t(9;22) / BCR-ABL1
questions.explanation: Malignant neutrophils in this disease lack the enzyme.

questions.question: Which finding best favors a benign leukemoid reaction over chronic myeloid leukemia in a patient with marked leukocytosis?
questions.explanation: Remember that the LAP score is the opposite in the benign condition.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the early pathogenesis of CML?
options: A block in differentiation at the promyelocyte stage
Decreased apoptosis due to BCL2 overexpression
A constitutively active tyrosine kinase drives proliferation and blocks apoptosis, while...
questions.explanation: This is why mature and maturing granulocytes fill the blood.

questions.question: A patient with CML in the chronic phase develops rapidly rising blasts, fever and bone pain. Into which diseases can this blast crisis transform?
questions.explanation: The triphasic course ends with a fatal transformation into an acute leukemia.

questions.question: Why does molecular detection of the BCR-ABL1 transcript directly guide therapy in CML?
options: It predicts response to anti-CD20 antibodies
It indicates the need for all-trans retinoic acid
It identifies a BCL2 inhibitor target
It identifies the exact target for tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib
questions.explanation: Think of the abnormal protein that the drug inhibits.

questions.question: Which finding on immunophenotyping definitively distinguishes CLL from mantle cell lymphoma, since both co-express CD5 with B-cell markers?
questions.explanation: Both share CD5, so look for the other marker that differs.

questions.question: Why are smudge cells seen on the peripheral smear of CLL?
options: They are apoptotic blasts with Auer rods
The fragile neoplastic lymphocytes burst during smear preparation
They are plasma cells producing excess immunoglobulin
questions.explanation: Mature-looking but fragile cells.

questions.question: CLL is primarily a disease of which pathogenic mechanism?
options: Maturation block at the promyelocyte stage
Marrow replacement by lymphoblasts with Notch1 mutations
questions.explanation: Cells accumulate because they do not die, not because they divide fast.

questions.question: A 72-year-old with CLL has recurrent bacterial infections and a falling hemoglobin with a positive direct antiglobulin test. Which pair of complications explains this picture?
options: Disseminated intravascular coagulation and leukemia cutis
Hypogammaglobulinemia and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
questions.explanation: One complication is immune deficiency, the other is immune dysregulation.

questions.question: What is the Philadelphia chromosome?
options: A shortened chromosome 9 formed by t(15;17)
A shortened chromosome 22 (22q-) carrying the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, formed by t(9;22)
A deletion of 13q found in CLL
questions.explanation: Chromosome 9 becomes 9q+ and the partner becomes the shortened one.

questions.question: Which laboratory panel is consistent with hemolytic anemia?
options: Reticulocytes low, LDH high, indirect bilirubin high, haptoglobin low
Reticulocytes high, LDH high, indirect bilirubin high, haptoglobin low
Reticulocytes high, LDH low, direct bilirubin high, haptoglobin high
Reticulocytes high, LDH normal, indirect bilirubin high, haptoglobin high
questions.explanation: The marrow compensates, and a protein that binds free hemoglobin is consumed.

questions.question: During a transfusion a patient develops cola-colored urine and severe back pain; haptoglobin is profoundly low. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Intravascular hemolysis with release of free hemoglobin into plasma
Ineffective erythropoiesis with death of precursors in the marrow
Aplastic marrow failure with low reticulocytes
questions.explanation: Where are the red cells lysed: inside the vessels or inside macrophages?

questions.question: What causes splenomegaly in chronic extravascular hemolysis?
options: Infiltration of the spleen by leukemic cells
Work hypertrophy of splenic macrophages that remove abnormal RBCs
questions.explanation: Think about which cells are doing the extra work.

questions.question: A 30-year-old has anemia, jaundice and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Which options are DAT-negative?

questions.question: Chronic hemolysis predisposes to which type of gallstones?
questions.explanation: Consider what accumulates in excess in chronic hemolysis.

questions.question: Which of the following is an extrinsic (acquired) cause of hemolytic anemia?
options: Mechanical fragmentation by a prosthetic cardiac valve
questions.explanation: The RBC itself is normal; the damage comes from outside.

questions.question: Which smear findings point to G6PD deficiency?
options: Heinz bodies with bite and blister cells
questions.explanation: Oxidative damage leaves characteristic marks on red cells.

questions.question: Which statement defines hemolytic anemia?
options: Premature destruction of red cells (lifespan under 120 days) with compensatory marrow...
questions.explanation: Short red cell survival, compensated by the marrow.

questions.question: What is the most common mechanism of hemolysis?
options: Extravascular, by macrophages in the spleen and liver
questions.explanation: RBCs are recognized as abnormal and phagocytosed.

questions.question: What is the classic triad of hemolytic anemia?
questions.explanation: Pallor, bilirubin and spleen.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue, craves ice and has spoon-shaped nails. Which laboratory pattern is expected?
options: Low MCV, low ferritin, high TIBC, transferrin saturation below 15%
Low MCV, high ferritin, low TIBC
High MCV, elevated homocysteine and MMA
Normal MCV, high LDH, low haptoglobin
questions.explanation: Think about what the liver does with transferrin when usable iron is scarce.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man has iron deficiency anemia. Which cause is most likely and should be sought first?
options: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss (ulcer, polyp or malignancy)
questions.explanation: Consider the most common cause in adults in developed countries.

questions.question: In the earliest stage of iron deficiency, which finding is present?
options: Microcytic hypochromic RBCs with pencil cells
Decreased ferritin with still-normal RBC morphology
Low serum iron and high TIBC with overt anemia
High ferritin with iron trapped in macrophages
questions.explanation: Marrow macrophages lose iron before the red cells change.

questions.question: Why are the red cells small and pale in iron deficiency anemia?
options: Insufficient iron limits heme synthesis, so erythroblasts undergo extra divisions to maintain...
Lack of thymidine delays DNA replication while the cytoplasm keeps growing
Excess unpaired globin chains damage the membrane and precursors
Hepcidin degrades ferroportin and blocks iron release from macrophages
questions.explanation: Compare with the cause of macrocytosis: here the problem is heme, not DNA synthesis.

questions.question: Which set of changes in serum iron, TIBC and transferrin saturation is expected in iron deficiency anemia?
options: Low iron, low TIBC, low transferrin saturation
High iron, low TIBC, high transferrin saturation
Low iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation
Low iron, normal TIBC, high transferrin saturation
questions.explanation: TIBC reflects transferrin made by the liver.

questions.question: Which pair of findings is expected in iron deficiency anemia but absent in anemia of chronic disease?
options: Low serum iron and mild anemia
questions.explanation: Look for tissue iron-deficit signs rather than general anemia symptoms.

questions.question: A blood smear shows microcytes with pencil and cigar cells and an elevated RDW. Which diagnosis is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Small, elongated cells with marked variation in size.

questions.question: Which finding marks the second stage of iron deficiency (iron-restricted erythropoiesis)?
options: Ferritin falls while RBC morphology remains normal
Erythroblasts undergo extra divisions to produce microcytic cells
Serum iron falls and TIBC rises, with fewer RBCs produced
Ferritin rises because iron is trapped in macrophages
questions.explanation: It comes after depletion of stores but before overt microcytic anemia.

questions.question: Which signs are iron-specific tissue deficits in iron deficiency anemia?
options: Koilonychia, angular stomatitis and a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis)
questions.explanation: Think of epithelial changes in nails, mouth corners and tongue.

questions.question: Which situation increases iron demand and can lead to iron deficiency anemia?
options: Pregnancy, infancy or rapid growth in adolescence
questions.explanation: Think of periods of increased blood volume and growth.

questions.question: A 70-year-old has anemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The marrow is hypercellular with dysplasia in more than one lineage. Which category and risk fit best?
options: Aplastic anemia; fat-replaced marrow and HSCT is curative
Myeloproliferative neoplasm; high counts with splenomegaly
Acute leukemia; abrupt blast accumulation without dysplasia
questions.explanation: Cytopenias despite a hypercellular marrow: what is wrong with the quality of hematopoiesis?

questions.question: What does pluripotency mean for hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)?
options: They can only produce red blood cells
They exist only in the thymus
They reside in the bone marrow and give rise to all lineages of mature blood cells
questions.explanation: Think of how many lineages arise from one cell.

questions.question: Which mature cells arise from the myeloid progenitor?
options: T cells and B cells only
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes come from the other branch.

questions.question: How do diseases of hematopoietic stem cells (clonal disorders) typically manifest?
options: As widespread abnormalities in blood cell production, either pancytopenia or excessive proliferation
As an isolated defect of a single mature cell membrane protein
As an inherited deficiency of one clotting factor
As a localized tumor without blood changes
questions.explanation: The stem cell sits at the root of every lineage.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four major categories of stem or progenitor cell disorders?
questions.explanation: Aplastic, myeloproliferative, myelodysplastic and acute leukemia make up the list.

questions.question: Which category is a syndrome of primary hematopoietic failure with profound pancytopenia?
questions.explanation: The marrow fails to produce cells.

questions.question: Mutated HSCs that overproduce one or more mature blood lineages (for example polycythemia vera) belong to which category?
questions.explanation: Overproduction of mature cells.

questions.question: How does the marrow of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) differ from that of aplastic anemia?
options: MDS marrow is empty of cells, aplastic marrow is packed with blasts
MDS marrow is hypercellular and dysplastic, whereas aplastic marrow is hypocellular and fatty
questions.explanation: Both give cytopenias, but the marrow cellularity is opposite.

questions.question: Which genes are the driver mutations in MDS?
options: Constitutively active tyrosine kinases such as JAK2 and BCR-ABL
Telomerase and DNA repair genes only
Splicing factors, epigenetic regulators and transcription factors involved in hematopoiesis
questions.explanation: Contrast with the tyrosine kinase drivers of MPNs.

questions.question: What do all subtypes of acute leukemia (AML, B-ALL, T-ALL) have in common?
options: Constitutively active BCR-ABL1 in every case
Mutations that interfere with hematopoietic stem cell differentiation
questions.explanation: A block in differentiation leads to blast accumulation.

questions.question: A 24-year-old presents with progressive pallor, petechiae and recurrent fever. CBC shows pancytopenia with a very low reticulocyte count, and the spleen is not palpable. Which bone marrow finding is expected?
options: Hypercellular marrow with dysplasia in one or more lineages
Markedly hypocellular marrow replaced by fat
Marrow packed with blasts and no fat spaces
questions.explanation: Look at the reticulocyte count and the absence of splenomegaly: is the marrow failing to produce or to mature?

questions.question: Which cytokines released by autoreactive TH1 cells suppress and destroy hematopoietic progenitors in aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Think of the cytokines typical of a TH1 cellular response.

questions.question: A patient with pancytopenia has teardrop-shaped red cells and early erythroid and myeloid precursors in the peripheral blood. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Myelophthisic anemia due to marrow infiltration (e.g., metastatic carcinoma)
Aplastic anemia, because precursors escape from the fatty marrow
Hypersplenism, because the enlarged spleen releases precursors
questions.explanation: What pushes immature cells into the blood when the marrow is crowded out?

questions.question: Which finding would argue AGAINST aplastic anemia in a patient with pancytopenia?
options: Onset after seronegative (non-A, non-B, non-C) hepatitis
Insidious onset with fever and mucosal bleeding
questions.explanation: Look for the sign that is characteristically absent in this disease.

questions.question: A 19-year-old has severe acquired aplastic anemia and an HLA-matched sibling. Which treatment is the curative option of choice?
options: ATG plus cyclosporine alone, since the disease is purely immune-mediated
questions.explanation: The goal is a cure, not just immune suppression, especially in young patients.

questions.question: Which agent causes aplastic anemia through an idiosyncratic (non-dose-related) reaction?
questions.explanation: Distinguish dose-related toxicity from an unpredictable individual reaction.

questions.question: Shortened telomeres in hematopoietic stem cells lead to aplastic anemia mainly through which mechanism?
options: Marrow infiltration by metastatic tumor cells
questions.explanation: This is an intrinsic mechanism, not an immune one.

questions.question: Which statement defines aplastic anemia?
options: Replacement of the marrow by metastatic carcinoma
Suppression of multipotent myeloid stem cells leading to marrow failure and pancytopenia
Ineffective hematopoiesis in a hypercellular dysplastic marrow
questions.explanation: Look for stem cell suppression and an empty marrow.

questions.question: A patient with pancytopenia and a chronically enlarged spleen is most likely to have which condition, and why?
options: Aplastic anemia, because the spleen is always enlarged
Myelophthisic anemia, because the spleen produces extra precursors
Hypersplenism, because the spleen removes excess formed elements, platelets in particular
questions.explanation: Splenomegaly is characteristically absent in aplastic anemia.

questions.question: What is the defining histologic feature of the aplastic anemia bone marrow?
options: Sheets of blasts with Auer rods
Obliterative fibrosis with dense megakaryocyte clusters
Marked hypocellularity with fat replacement, often more than 90% of the marrow space
questions.explanation: The marrow is described as empty.

questions.question: Which statement describes the unifying molecular hallmark of classic myeloproliferative neoplasms?
options: Acquired somatic mutations causing constitutive activation of tyrosine kinase signaling
Inherited defects in DNA repair factors
Mutations in splicing factors causing ineffective hematopoiesis
Antigenic alteration of stem cells provoking a T-cell attack
questions.explanation: Think about independence from growth factors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a shared feature of the classic myeloproliferative neoplasms?
options: Tendency to progress to marrow fibrosis (spent phase)
Variable risk of transformation to AML
Early profound pancytopenia from suppression of residual marrow
questions.explanation: The proliferating cells in these diseases go outside the marrow rather than suppress the rest.

questions.question: Mutated CALR, which stimulates the thrombopoietin receptor, is characteristic of which myeloproliferative neoplasms?
options: Chronic myeloid leukemia and polycythemia vera
questions.explanation: Follow the thrombopoietin pathway: which neoplasms depend on megakaryocytes/platelets?

questions.question: A 48-year-old has splenomegaly and WBC 80,000/µL with neutrophilia, marked left shift and fewer than 10% blasts. Which pair is correct?
options: BCR-ABL fusion, t(9;22); treated with ABL kinase inhibitors
JAK2 V617F; treated mainly with phlebotomy
CALR mutation; treated with ATG and cyclosporine
MPL mutation; treated with HSCT as the only option
questions.explanation: The genetic lesion here is a fusion gene, not a point mutation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with no prior hematologic disease has progressive anemia and increasing splenomegaly. The smear shows leukoerythroblastosis; the marrow shows obliterative fibrosis driven by megakaryocyte cytokines. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The oldest age group and the most extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis.

questions.question: A patient has a platelet count near 1,000,000/mm³ with giant platelets and massively increased marrow megakaryocytes. Hematocrit is normal, there is no BCR-ABL, and no marrow fibrosis. Which diagnosis fits, and what is notable about it?
options: Primary myelofibrosis; the oldest age group with obliterative fibrosis
Polycythemia vera; panmyelosis dominated by red cells
Chronic myeloid leukemia; Philadelphia chromosome in about 90%
Essential thrombocythemia; the rarest MPN and often a diagnosis of exclusion
questions.explanation: The dominant lineage is platelets and there is no fibrosis.

questions.question: Which statement defines myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs)?
options: Disorders of ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias
Clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders with proliferation of one or more mature myeloid lineages
questions.explanation: They are also called chronic myeloproliferative disorders.

questions.question: How do MPNs differ from myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) in hematopoiesis and blood counts?
options: Both show high counts with splenomegaly
Both show pancytopenia with an empty marrow
MPN: increased production and high counts; MDS: ineffective production with cytopenias
questions.explanation: One overproduces, the other fails to mature.

questions.question: Which marrow and blood picture fits CML?
options: More than 20% blasts with Auer rods
100% cellular marrow with a massively increased M:E ratio and left-shifted neutrophils but under...
Predominant dense fibrosis with teardrop cells
questions.explanation: All cell lines are increased, but blasts remain few.

questions.question: Which feature is characteristic of primary myelofibrosis (PMF)?
options: Oldest age group of the MPNs, with the most extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis
Youngest age group of the MPNs
Marrow that is the primary site of hematopoiesis
questions.explanation: The marrow is not the main site of blood production here.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with polycythemia vera has plethora and headaches. What is the mainstay of initial therapy and its target?
options: Hydroxyurea as first-line, targeting a normal platelet count
Ruxolitinib as first-line, to suppress JAK2
questions.explanation: The main treatment physically removes red cells.

questions.question: Which best explains the markedly low serum EPO in polycythemia vera?
options: Destruction of renal EPO-producing cells by autoreactive T cells
Loss of the EPO receptor on erythroid precursors
Autonomous JAK2-driven red cell production; the expanded red cell mass suppresses renal EPO via...
Ectopic EPO secretion by a tumor
questions.explanation: Ask what controls red cell production instead of EPO, and what the expanded red cell mass does to the kidney.

questions.question: Which laboratory pattern favors polycythemia vera over secondary erythrocytosis from chronic hypoxia?
options: High EPO, JAK2 negative, no splenomegaly
Low EPO, JAK2 negative, normal platelets
Low EPO, JAK2 V617F positive, with leukocytosis and thrombocytosis
questions.explanation: Compare primary (clonal) and reactive causes by EPO level, mutation status and other lineages.

questions.question: A patient with polycythemia vera complains of intense itching after a hot bath. What is the best explanation?
options: Uric acid deposition in the skin
Cytokine release by autoreactive TH1 cells
questions.explanation: Focus on the cells raised in the peripheral blood other than red cells.

questions.question: Why may patients with polycythemia vera have epistaxis or GI bleeding despite thrombocytosis?
questions.explanation: The platelet count is high, but what about their function?

questions.question: A patient with polycythemia vera for 12 years develops worsening anemia, leukoerythroblastosis and massive splenomegaly, and no longer needs phlebotomy. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Development of secondary erythrocytosis from hypoxia
questions.explanation: After years of overproduction the marrow 'burns out'.

questions.question: What does the JAK2 V617F mutation do in polycythemia vera?
options: It makes JAK2 constitutively active, so erythroid signalling occurs even without erythropoietin
It blocks maturation at the promyelocyte stage
questions.explanation: Signals without the ligand.

questions.question: What is meant by panmyelosis in polycythemia vera?
options: Proliferation of all three myeloid lineages, with red cells dominant
questions.explanation: Despite the name, other lines rise too.

questions.question: Which unusual thrombosis is peculiarly associated with polycythemia vera?
questions.explanation: A liver vein.

questions.question: In what proportion of polycythemia vera patients does the spent phase (post-PV myelofibrosis) develop?
questions.explanation: After years of overproduction, the marrow burns out.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy has recurrent hemarthroses after minor trauma. His maternal uncle had a similar problem. Which screening profile is expected?
options: Prolonged bleeding time and PTT with normal PT
Prolonged PT and PTT with low platelets
Normal bleeding time, platelet count and PT; prolonged PTT
questions.explanation: Think of factor VIII and the intrinsic pathway.

questions.question: A woman who is a carrier of hemophilia A has a son with a normal partner. What is the chance that the son is affected?
questions.explanation: The disease is X-linked recessive.

questions.question: A boy with joint and muscle bleeds has the same screening results as hemophilia A, but the FVIII assay is normal. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
options: Factor IX assay showing decreased activity
questions.explanation: Also known as Christmas disease.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman has epistaxis and menorrhagia. Tests show prolonged bleeding time and PTT, normal PT and platelet count, and defective ristocetin aggregation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding with both bleeding time and PTT prolonged.

questions.question: Why is the PTT prolonged in von Willebrand disease even though the factor VIII gene is normal?
options: vWF is a cofactor for thrombin in the common pathway
vWF is consumed by widespread microvascular thrombosis
vWF is the carrier for factor VIII, so a deficiency of vWF lowers FVIII activity
questions.explanation: Think of vWF's two functions.

questions.question: A patient has a complete quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor. Which type is this?
questions.explanation: Type 1 is partial and type 2 is qualitative.

questions.question: Which of the following is a chronic cause of DIC?
questions.explanation: The other options are acute triggers.

questions.question: Which laboratory profile is expected in DIC?
options: Low platelets, normal PT/PTT, normal fibrinogen
Normal platelets, prolonged PTT only, increased fibrinogen
Low platelets, prolonged PT/PTT/TT, reduced fibrinogen and increased D-dimer
High platelets, shortened PT/PTT, decreased D-dimer
questions.explanation: Consumption of factors plus fibrinolysis.

questions.question: A septic patient develops oliguria, confusion and diffuse bleeding, with schistocytes on the blood film. Why does he bleed despite widespread microvascular thrombosis?
options: He has an inherited deficiency of factor VIII
Aspirin-like inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase in platelets
Clotting factors and platelets are consumed, and plasmin generates fibrin split products that...
questions.explanation: Thrombosis and bleeding coexist because of consumption and fibrinolysis.

questions.question: Which components does normal hemostasis depend on?
options: Red cells and white cells only
Blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors, fibrinolysis and natural anticoagulant inhibitors
questions.explanation: Several systems cooperate.

questions.question: A patient with severe thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic changes and neurologic symptoms is diagnosed with TTP. A colleague suggests a platelet transfusion for the low count. What is the correct response?
options: Transfuse only if the count is below 50,000/µL
Avoid it, because it is contraindicated in TTP and fuels the coagulopathy
Transfuse routinely, because the count is low
Transfuse only after confirming a normal PT and PTT
questions.explanation: Low counts are generally not corrected by transfusion unless bleeding or below 10,000/µL, with this key exception.

questions.question: A child has ecchymoses and epistaxis. The smear shows giant platelets with thrombocytopenia, and ristocetin-induced aggregation is impaired. Which defect is responsible?
questions.explanation: These receptors mediate adhesion through von Willebrand factor.

questions.question: Platelet aggregation tests in a patient with petechiae and purpura show no aggregation with ADP, thrombin, collagen or epinephrine. Which disorder and defect fit?
options: Storage pool disease; absent dense granules
Gray platelet syndrome; alpha granule deficiency
questions.explanation: This is a defect of primary aggregation, which depends on the fibrinogen receptor.

questions.question: A patient with ecchymoses, epistaxis and hematuria has reduced collagen-induced aggregation and no secondary aggregation response to ADP and epinephrine. What is the underlying abnormality?
questions.explanation: Dense granules store the substances released for secondary aggregation.

questions.question: Large platelets with thrombocytopenia and decreased PF4 and β-thromboglobulin are found in which condition?
questions.explanation: PF4 and β-thromboglobulin are stored in one specific type of granule.

questions.question: Why does a single dose of aspirin impair platelet function for 3 to 7 days?
options: It irreversibly inactivates cyclo-oxygenase, so TXA₂ formation and the ADP release reaction are...
It reversibly blocks GP IIb-IIIa receptors
It depletes dense granule stores permanently in the megakaryocyte
It destroys von Willebrand factor in plasma
questions.explanation: Platelets have no nucleus to synthesize new enzyme.

questions.question: Which of the following is stored in platelet alpha granules?
questions.explanation: Dense granules hold ADP, ATP, Ca and serotonin; lysosomes hold hydrolases.

questions.question: Which platelet glycoprotein binds collagen?
questions.explanation: Remember the ligands: vWF, thrombin, fibrinogen and collagen each have their own receptor.

questions.question: Which of the following is a cause of thrombocytopenia due to decreased production?
questions.explanation: The liver produces thrombopoietin.

questions.question: Which of the following is an acquired platelet functional disorder?
questions.explanation: The other options are inherited.

questions.question: A patient with a prolonged bleeding time is taking a drug known to interfere with platelet function. What is the next step in the diagnostic flowchart?
options: Immediately perform a bone marrow biopsy
Order factor VIII and IX assays
Discontinue the drug and repeat the bleeding time; if it corrects, no further evaluation is needed
questions.explanation: Look for a reversible, drug-induced cause first.

questions.question: Why is von Willebrand disease described as strictly not a platelet disorder?
options: The platelets are absent from blood
The abnormality is quantitative or qualitative, and lies in von Willebrand factor, not in the...
It affects only coagulation factor IX
It is caused by a defect of GP IIb-IIIa
questions.explanation: The defect is in a plasma protein.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents with painless, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, weight loss and intermittent fever lasting a few days followed by 1–2 afebrile weeks. A node biopsy shows large binucleated cells with an owl-eye appearance. Which immunophenotype is expected in these cells?
questions.explanation: The fever pattern is named after Pel and Ebstein.

questions.question: Why do most cells in a Hodgkin lymphoma node turn out to be non-neoplastic?
options: Reed-Sternberg cells differentiate into eosinophils and plasma cells
The neoplastic cells are mostly lost through extensive apoptosis
Reed-Sternberg cells undergo clonal expansion into lymphocytes
Reed-Sternberg cells secrete cytokines such as IL-5 and TGF-β that recruit a reactive...
questions.explanation: The rare neoplastic cell orchestrates its own background.

questions.question: A lymph node biopsy shows collagen bands dividing the node into nodules, with lacunar cells in a mixed inflammatory background. Which Hodgkin lymphoma subtype is this?
questions.explanation: The architectural clue is in the name, and it is also the most common subtype.

questions.question: Which pair of Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes is strongly associated with EBV?
questions.explanation: One has a diffuse mixed background, the other is rare with fibrosis.

questions.question: A 68-year-old HIV-positive patient has a rare Hodgkin lymphoma subtype with a diffuse inflammatory background, fibrosis and pleomorphic variants of RS cells. What is the expected prognosis?
options: The worst prognosis among the Hodgkin subtypes
Good prognosis, because EBV-associated tumors respond to antivirals
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are scarce in this subtype.

questions.question: Which histologic description fits lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin lymphoma, and what is its prognosis?
options: Numerous reactive lymphocytes with scattered RS cells; worst prognosis
Numerous reactive lymphocytes with scattered RS cells; excellent prognosis
Collagen bands with lacunar cells; excellent prognosis
Diffuse fibrosis with pleomorphic RS cells; excellent prognosis
questions.explanation: The name describes the background cells.

questions.question: On what does the WHO classification of lymphomas rely?
options: Serum LDH level and age only
Morphology, cell of origin, immunophenotype (CD markers) and genetics
Site of the lymph node group only
questions.explanation: Several features are combined.

questions.question: What is the age distribution of Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Bimodal, with peaks in young adulthood and again after 55 years
questions.explanation: Two peaks.

questions.question: Which Hodgkin lymphoma subtype shows a lymphocyte background in a diffuse pattern, rare RS cells and a 'popcorn' variant?
questions.explanation: Named after the background cells and the variant cell shape.

questions.question: Which gross description fits an involved node in Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Enlarged, firm and discrete, later adherent from capsular invasion, with a homogeneous...
Soft, necrotic and hemorrhagic with a starry sky cut surface
questions.explanation: Early discrete, late adherent.

questions.question: Which feature best favors Hodgkin lymphoma over non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Localized to a single axial node group with orderly, contiguous spread
Frequent extranodal involvement such as GI tract, skin or brain
Non-contiguous, random spread to multiple peripheral nodes
A tumor mass composed entirely of neoplastic lymphoid cells
questions.explanation: Think about how the disease moves from one node group to the next.

questions.question: What is the molecular consequence of t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma?
options: Cyclin D1 is fused to the IgH locus, driving G1-to-S progression
c-MYC is overexpressed, causing rapid cell-cycle proliferation
BCL6 is dysregulated, producing large proliferating cells
BCL2 is placed next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus, causing overexpression and...
questions.explanation: Germinal center B-cells fail to die and accumulate.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman has painless, generalized, waxing and waning lymphadenopathy for years. Biopsy shows nodular effacement of the architecture. Which immunophenotype is expected?
options: CD19+, CD20+, CD10+, surface IgM+ with Ki-67 near 100%
questions.explanation: This is a germinal center B-cell tumor with an anti-apoptotic marker.

questions.question: A patient with long-standing follicular lymphoma develops a rapidly enlarging mass with fever and night sweats. Biopsy shows a diffuse pattern of large cells with a high Ki-67 index. What has happened?
options: Transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
questions.explanation: An indolent lymphoma can become aggressive.

questions.question: Which statement about diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is correct?
options: It is the most common NHL overall and is caused by dysregulation of BCL6, BCL2 or MYC
It is the most common indolent NHL and is driven by t(14;18)
It is driven by t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression
It is defined by CD30+ and CD15+ giant cells
questions.explanation: Do not confuse the most common NHL overall with the most common indolent one.

questions.question: A biopsy shows sheets of intermediate cells with a high mitotic rate, extensive apoptosis and macrophages creating a starry sky pattern; Ki-67 is nearly 100%. Which translocation is expected?
questions.explanation: Starry sky and a near 100% proliferation index point to the most aggressive B-cell lymphoma.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child presents with an abdominal mass in the ileocecal region. Biopsy shows a highly aggressive B-cell lymphoma with surface IgM and CD10. Which form of the disease is this?
questions.explanation: The African form presents elsewhere, with jaw and facial bone lesions.

questions.question: In mantle cell lymphoma, how does t(11;14) promote tumor growth?
options: It fuses cyclin D1 to the IgH locus, and its overexpression drives G1-to-S phase progression
It places BCL2 next to the IgH locus, blocking apoptosis
It overexpresses c-MYC, driving rapid proliferation with extensive apoptosis
It creates a constitutively active tyrosine kinase
questions.explanation: The overexpressed protein regulates the cell cycle checkpoint.

questions.question: A B-cell neoplasm is CD5+ and cyclin D1+. What is the expected CD23 result, and what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CD23 is the marker that separates this tumor from CLL.

questions.question: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma in children typically presents with which lesions?
questions.explanation: The sporadic form is the abdominal one.

questions.question: Which mechanism explains macrocytosis in megaloblastic anemia?
options: Excess unpaired globin chains aggregate and damage the membrane
Insufficient iron limits heme synthesis and causes extra divisions
Lack of B12/folate delays thymidine and DNA synthesis while RNA and protein synthesis continue
Hepcidin degrades ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages
questions.explanation: The nucleus and cytoplasm mature at different rates.

questions.question: A 55-year-old strict vegan has numbness, tingling, loss of vibration and position sense, and ataxia. Which laboratory pattern is expected?
options: MCV above 110 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils, elevated homocysteine and elevated MMA
Low MCV, low ferritin, high TIBC
High MCV, elevated homocysteine, normal MMA
Normal MCV, high ferritin, low TIBC
questions.explanation: Neurological involvement points to one of the two vitamins.

questions.question: An elderly alcoholic with a poor diet has MCV 112 fL and hypersegmented neutrophils, with no neurological symptoms. Which marker pattern is expected?
questions.explanation: One vitamin is needed for the methylmalonic acid pathway; the other is not.

questions.question: Why are LDH and bilirubin markedly elevated in megaloblastic anemia?
options: Extravascular destruction of spherocytes in the spleen
Heavy death of erythroid precursors inside the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis)
questions.explanation: Where do the abnormal red cell precursors die?

questions.question: Which of the following causes megaloblastic anemia through vitamin B12 deficiency?
options: Poor diet in an alcoholic patient
Crohn disease with terminal ileum resection
questions.explanation: The other options are classic causes of the other vitamin deficiency.

questions.question: Which clinical sign of megaloblastic anemia reflects mild jaundice from intramarrow cell destruction?
questions.explanation: Pallor combined with a yellowish tint.

questions.question: Which statement defines megaloblastic anemia?
options: A microcytic hypochromic anemia due to iron depletion
A macrocytic anemia with large abnormal RBC precursors (megaloblasts) in the marrow due to...
A hemolytic anemia due to spherocytes
A normocytic anemia due to IL-6 and hepcidin
questions.explanation: The defect is in DNA synthesis.

questions.question: Which smear finding is characteristic of megaloblastic anemia?
options: Macrocytes and neutrophils with more than five nuclear lobes
questions.explanation: Look at the neutrophil nuclei.

questions.question: Pernicious anemia causes vitamin B12 deficiency through which mechanism?
options: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells / intrinsic factor
questions.explanation: Without intrinsic factor B12 cannot be absorbed.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes B12 deficiency from folate deficiency clinically?
options: Macrocytosis occurs only in folate deficiency
Hypersegmented neutrophils occur only in B12 deficiency
Folate deficiency causes ataxia and dementia
Neurological signs such as subacute combined degeneration of the cord occur only in B12 deficiency
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency does not cause neurological symptoms.

questions.question: Which finding on lymph node histology favors malignant follicular lymphoma over reactive follicular hyperplasia?
options: A distinct and well-preserved mantle zone
Marked variation in follicle size and shape
Absent or rare tingible-body macrophages due to decreased apoptosis
questions.explanation: BCL2 overexpression reduces cell death, so there is little debris to phagocytose.

questions.question: A lymph node shows preserved architecture, follicles of varying size and shape with polarized light and dark zones, a preserved mantle zone and a polyclonal cell mix. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Benign and reversible; B-lymphocyte activation, as in rheumatoid arthritis or early HIV.

questions.question: A 20-year-old with fever, sore throat and generalized lymphadenopathy from a viral infection has a node biopsy showing expansion of the interfollicular zones. Which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: The paracortex is the T-cell zone.

questions.question: A pathologist examining axillary nodes finds expansion of the subcapsular and medullary sinuses by macrophages. What should be suspected?
options: A nearby malignancy being drained, such as breast carcinoma
questions.explanation: Also called reticular hyperplasia.

questions.question: A 65-year-old presents with bone pain, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency and anemia. The blood smear shows rouleaux formation. Which description of the underlying neoplasm is correct?
options: Clonal immature lymphoblasts with TdT positivity
Clonal malignant plasma cells secreting a single homogeneous immunoglobulin (M protein)
Reed-Sternberg cells secreting IL-5 and TGF-β
Mature B-cells with smudge cells and CD5+/CD23+
questions.explanation: The features listed form the CRAB criteria.

questions.question: Which histologic picture fits acute nonspecific lymphadenitis?
options: Effaced architecture with sheets of monotonous cells
Starry sky pattern with Ki-67 near 100%
Swollen, engorged, painful nodes with large germinal centers, many mitoses and macrophages...
questions.explanation: Reactive and painful.

questions.question: Which conditions are associated with follicular hyperplasia?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis and early HIV (B-lymphocyte activation)
questions.explanation: B-cell activation.

questions.question: Which feature favors reactive hyperplasia over malignant lymphoma?
options: Prominent tingible-body macrophages from high apoptosis and phagocytosis
questions.explanation: Malignant follicular lymphoma has decreased apoptosis because of BCL2.

questions.question: What is the cellular composition of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia compared with lymphoma?
options: Polyclonal, a heterogeneous mix of cells at different stages of maturation
questions.explanation: Malignant lymphoma is the monoclonal one.

questions.question: What is the M protein in multiple myeloma?
options: A single homogeneous immunoglobulin secreted by a clonal population of malignant plasma cells
A heterogeneous mix of immunoglobulins from reactive B cells
An enzyme released by dying red cells
A cytokine secreted by Reed-Sternberg cells
questions.explanation: Monoclonal.

questions.question: Which best describes the molecular defect in sickle cell disease?
options: Deletion of one to four α-globin genes on chromosome 16
Valine replaced by glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
Frameshift in the β gene causing absent β⁰ production
Missense mutation in the β-globin gene on chromosome 11 replacing glutamic acid with valine at...
questions.explanation: Pay attention to the direction of the amino acid change and the chain involved.

questions.question: A healthy 25-year-old has sickle cell trait (HbAS). What does hemoglobin electrophoresis show?
questions.explanation: The trait keeps one normal β-globin allele.

questions.question: A metabisulfite sickling test is positive. What does this mean?
options: Sickling can be induced, but trait and disease cannot be distinguished without electrophoresis...
questions.explanation: It is a screening test, not the definitive one.

questions.question: Which process converts reversibly sickled cells into irreversibly sickled cells?
options: Complement fixation on the RBC surface
Aggregation of excess unpaired α chains
Oxidant damage with Heinz body formation
Repeated deoxygenation cycles with K⁺ and water efflux causing dehydration and membrane damage
questions.explanation: Think about cell hydration and the membrane.

questions.question: A 20-year-old with HbSS presents with chest pain, fever, hypoxemia and new pulmonary infiltrates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This complication is the leading cause of death in the disease.

questions.question: Howell-Jolly bodies on the smear of a patient with sickle cell disease indicate what?
options: Functional asplenia (autosplenectomy) with high risk of encapsulated bacterial infection
questions.explanation: Repeated infarctions have affected one organ by childhood.

questions.question: A teenager with HbSS has hip pain; a pelvic X-ray shows femoral head changes. Which complication is this?
questions.explanation: Think about downstream ischemia of bone.

questions.question: What is the inheritance and genotype of sickle cell disease?
options: Autosomal dominant; HbAS is severe disease
Mitochondrial; passed only by the mother
Autosomal recessive; homozygous HbSS, while heterozygous HbAS is sickle cell trait and largely...
questions.explanation: Both copies of the β-globin gene carry the mutation.

questions.question: Why does deoxygenated HbS distort the red cell?
options: It fragments into free α chains
It binds complement on the cell surface
It exposes hydrophobic patches and polymerizes into long stiff chains
questions.explanation: Valine is hydrophobic.

questions.question: Which events trigger vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation: Think of situations that favor sickling.

questions.question: In β-thalassemia, which excess chain aggregates and damages the red cell membrane?
questions.explanation: The unaffected chain is left without a partner.

questions.question: A 25-year-old has mild microcytic anemia: MCV 62 fL, RBC 5.8 × 10¹²/L and normal ferritin. Which diagnosis and confirmation fit best?
options: Iron deficiency anemia; low serum ferritin
β-thalassemia trait; electrophoresis showing raised HbA2 and HbF
Anemia of chronic disease; high ferritin with low TIBC
questions.explanation: Calculate MCV divided by RBC count.

questions.question: Which test confirms α-thalassemia trait in an adult?
questions.explanation: Adult electrophoresis is often normal in this form.

questions.question: A Mediterranean child becomes severely anemic and transfusion-dependent at 6–9 months of age. Why do symptoms appear at this age?
options: Fetal hemoglobin declines and β-chain production becomes necessary
The spleen begins destroying red cells at that age
questions.explanation: Think about which hemoglobin the infant relies on early in life.

questions.question: A patient with β-thalassemia major receives regular transfusions. Which statement about iron therapy is correct?
options: Iron supplements should be given routinely to correct the microcytosis
Iron should not be given unless iron deficiency coexists, given the risk of iron overload
Iron is indicated because ferritin is typically low
Iron should be given only after HbA2 normalizes
questions.explanation: Consider both the transfusions and the normal or elevated iron studies.

questions.question: Why do target cells form in thalassemia?
options: Excess cell membrane relative to the reduced hemoglobin volume
Precipitated oxidized hemoglobin attached to the membrane
questions.explanation: Compare the amount of membrane with the amount of hemoglobin.

questions.question: What defines the thalassemia syndromes?
options: Inherited quantitative reduction or absence of α or β globin chain synthesis
A structural amino acid substitution in the β chain
questions.explanation: The globin chain is normal in structure but made in reduced amounts.

questions.question: What is the genetic basis of α-thalassemia?
options: Point mutations in the β gene on chromosome 11
A missense mutation replacing glutamic acid with valine
Deletion of one to four α genes on chromosome 16
questions.explanation: Alpha involves deletions, beta involves point mutations.

questions.question: A Mentzer index (MCV/RBC count) below 13 suggests which diagnosis?
options: Iron deficiency anemia rather than thalassemia
Thalassemia trait rather than iron deficiency
questions.explanation: In thalassemia the RBC count is normal or high.

questions.question: Which skeletal changes occur in β-thalassemia major?
options: Crew-cut skull and chipmunk facies from massive marrow expansion
questions.explanation: The marrow expands to compensate.

questions.question: If a patient has Multi-drug resistant malaria, what is the primary curative choice?

questions.question: What is the primary treatment for Toxoplasmosis in a non-pregnant patient?

questions.question: What is the drug of choice for a pregnant woman diagnosed with Toxoplasmosis?
questions.explanation: Correct Answer: Spiramycin

questions.question: What does Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) cause?

questions.question: How is Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) treated?

questions.question: Which of the following drugs acts as an irreversible COX-1 inhibitor, decreasing TXA2 synthesis?

questions.question: Which of the following P2Y12 inhibitors is administered intravenously (IV) only and has a reversible effect?
questions.explanation: Correct Answer: Cangrelor

questions.question: Which antiplatelet drug is a prodrug that requires hepatic activation via the CYP2C19 enzyme?

questions.question: Which of the following drugs is a monoclonal antibody that irreversibly blocks GP IIb/IIIa receptors?
